t: Rearrange Words in a Sentence — Stable Sort by Length
o: We must split a sentence into words, sort them by length (ties keep original order), then rejoin with the first word capitalized and the rest lowercase. Example 2 shows the tie rule: 'keep', 'calm', 'code' all have length 4 and stay in original relative order. Example 1/3 show we must lowercase everything except the new first word. Constraints allow up to $10^5$ characters, so an $O(n \log n)$ sort is fine; a naive approach that repeatedly scans for the shortest remaining word would be $O(n^2)$ in word count and risky at scale.
k: Python's sorted() is stable, so sorting by key=len alone preserves original order for equal lengths.
In C++/Java/JS use stable_sort / Arrays.sort with index tiebreak / decorate-sort-undecorate to guarantee stability.
Handle casing: lowercase all words first, capitalize only after rejoining.

a.i: Split the sentence into words, sort them by length using a stable sort so ties retain original order, then rebuild the sentence: lowercase every word, capitalize the first character of the result. Stability is exactly what the problem's tie rule demands.
s: Split text on spaces into a list of words.
Lowercase each word and join with single spaces.
Capitalize the first letter of the joined string and return it.
a.t: O(n log n) where n is total characters — splitting is O(n), sorting O(n log n), joining O(n).
a.sp: O(n) for the word list and result string.

a.i: Word lengths are bounded by n, so we can bucket words by length and concatenate buckets in increasing length order. This achieves linear time since no comparison-based sort is needed, and buckets naturally preserve original order within each length.
s: Split text into words; find the maximum word length m.
Create m+1 buckets of lists of lowercased words.
Append each word to its length bucket (original order preserved).
Concatenate buckets from length 1 to m with spaces.
Capitalize the first character and return.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to bucket, one pass over buckets to join; no comparison sort needed.

w: In an interview, lead with the stable-sort solution (Approach 1) since it directly maps to the problem statement, then mention bucket sort as an optimization when asked about complexity. Pitfalls: forgetting to lowercase the original capital letter before rejoining, capitalizing the wrong position, and relying on unstable sorts (C++ std::sort, JS default sort on some engines historically) without an explicit tiebreak. Edge cases: single-word sentence, all words same length, maximum-length input. Follow-ups: what if memory is limited (streaming/bucketing helps), or if the tie rule changed to reverse order (just flip the comparator).
